exercises.objective: Compute a radial basis function feature value.
exercises.prompt: For an RBF feature $\phi_j(x)=e^{-\frac12\|x-c_j\|^2}$ with $x=(1,1)$ and center $c_j=(0,0)$, compute $\phi_j(x)$. Enter a decimal.
hints: $\phi_j(x)\approx0.3679$. (Independently verified with NumPy while authoring this module.)

exercises.objective: Compute estimator variance for a simple 1D regression case and connect it to overfitting.
exercises.prompt: For standardized 1D data with $X^\top X=n$ (so $\text{Var}\{\hat\beta\}=\sigma^2/n$), $\sigma^2=4$, $n=100$: compute $\text{Var}\{\hat\beta\}$. Enter a decimal.
hints: $\text{Var}\{\hat\beta\}=0.04$. More data ($n$ larger) directly reduces estimator variance, exactly the 'more data means less overfitting' intuition, made precise.

exercises.objective: Explain why lasso performs feature selection while ridge does not.
exercises.prompt: Explain, in terms of the two penalty functions' shapes (not just 'lasso uses absolute value'), why L1 (lasso) regularization tends to produce exactly-zero coefficients while L2 (ridge) does not.
hints: Ridge's penalty $\beta_j^2$ is smooth and has zero slope exactly at $\beta_j=0$: shrinking a small $\beta_j$ further toward zero costs less and less penalty-gradient the closer it gets, so the optimizer has little pressure to push it all the way to exactly zero.

Lasso's penalty $|\beta_j|$ has a constant-magnitude slope everywhere except at $\beta_j=0$, where it's non-differentiable (a sharp corner): this constant 'pull' toward zero doesn't weaken as $\beta_j$ shrinks, so it's entirely plausible for the optimum to land exactly at the corner, $\beta_j=0$, if the data doesn't provide enough gradient from the loss term to overcome that pull.

This is why lasso performs automatic feature selection (some $\beta_j$ become exactly zero, dropping that feature entirely) while ridge only ever shrinks coefficients toward zero without eliminating any of them.

exercises.objective: Explain why training error cannot be used to choose the regularization strength lambda.
exercises.prompt: Explain precisely why picking $\lambda$ to minimize training error always gives $\lambda=0$, and why that's the wrong choice.
hints: Training error is $\sum_i(y_i-\phi(x_i)^\top\beta)^2$ alone; adding any regularization term can only ever pull $\beta$ away from the unregularized least-squares minimizer, which is exactly the $\beta$ that minimizes training error by definition.
So for any $\lambda>0$, training error is (weakly) worse than at $\lambda=0$; minimizing training error over choices of $\lambda$ therefore always selects $\lambda=0$, no exceptions.

But $\lambda=0$ is exactly the no-regularization, maximal-estimator-variance, most-overfitting-prone setting; cross-validation instead estimates error on held-out data the model didn't fit, which genuinely can get worse as $\lambda\to0$ (overfitting) and worse again as $\lambda\to\infty$ (underfitting), giving an actual, non-degenerate criterion for choosing $\lambda$.

exercises.objective: Derive the binary logistic regression gradient from its negative-log-likelihood loss.
exercises.prompt: Starting from $L(\beta)=-\sum_i[y_i\log p_i+(1-y_i)\log(1-p_i)]+\lambda\|\beta\|^2$ with $p_i=\sigma(\phi(x_i)^\top\beta)$, and using $\sigma'(z)=\sigma(z)(1-\sigma(z))$ (ML-03), derive $\nabla_\beta L=X^\top(p-y)+2\lambda\beta$.
hints: For one data point, differentiate w.r.t. $\beta$ using the chain rule through $p_i=\sigma(z_i)$, $z_i=\phi(x_i)^\top\beta$: $\frac{\partial}{\partial\beta}\big[y_i\log p_i+(1-y_i)\log(1-p_i)\big] = \Big[\frac{y_i}{p_i}-\frac{1-y_i}{1-p_i}\Big]\,p_i(1-p_i)\,\phi(x_i)$.

Simplify the bracket: $\Big[\frac{y_i}{p_i}-\frac{1-y_i}{1-p_i}\Big]p_i(1-p_i) = y_i(1-p_i)-(1-y_i)p_i = y_i-p_i$. So the per-point derivative of $-[y_i\log p_i+(1-y_i)\log(1-p_i)]$ w.r.t. $\beta$ is $(p_i-y_i)\phi(x_i)$.

Summing over all $i$ and adding the regularization term's derivative $2\lambda\beta$: $\nabla_\beta L=\sum_i(p_i-y_i)\phi(x_i)+2\lambda\beta=X^\top(p-y)+2\lambda\beta$ (stacking $\phi(x_i)^\top$ as rows of $X$). (Independently verified symbolically with SymPy while authoring this module.)
